original_question: Characterize the numerical semigroups that can be expressed as quotients of complete intersection numerical semigroups by a positive integer.
target_in_paper: Section 5, unnumbered open question immediately after the definition of complete intersection numerical semigroups: "What semigroups can be expressed as the quotient of a complete intersection by a positive integer?"
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's intended target very closely. It correctly identifies the ambient objects as numerical semigroups, the operation as quotient by a positive integer, and the source class as complete intersection numerical semigroups. It is essentially a stand-alone restatement of the first of the two unnumbered questions posed in Section 5.
missing_details: Make the existential quantifiers explicit: for a target numerical semigroup T, ask whether there exist a complete intersection numerical semigroup S and a positive integer p such that T=S/p.
Define the quotient operation using the paper's notation: S/p := {x in N : p x in S}.
State the ambient convention N={0,1,2,...} and that all semigroups under discussion are numerical semigroups, i.e. cofinite additive submonoids of N containing 0.
If full self-containment is desired, define 'complete intersection' as a numerical semigroup whose minimal presentation has cardinality e(S)-1, where e(S) is the embedding dimension.
Avoid merging this with the neighboring but distinct question in the paper about the least Frobenius variety containing all complete intersection numerical semigroups.
Do not broaden it to quotients of embedding-dimension-three semigroups or to symmetric semigroups in general; those are nearby themes, not this exact target.
refined_question: Which numerical semigroups T⊆N arise as quotients of complete intersection numerical semigroups by positive integers? Equivalently stated in fully explicit form: characterize all numerical semigroups T for which there exist a complete intersection numerical semigroup S⊆N and an integer p≥1 such that T=S/p:={x∈N: px∈S}.
justification: The paper does not attach a number to this problem; the nearest official formulation is the unnumbered open question in Section 5. Your draft captures that question almost verbatim, so only definitional material needed for stand-alone precision had to be supplied. The key hidden assumptions come from two nearby places in the paper: Section 3 introduces the quotient S/p, and Section 5 defines complete intersections via minimal presentations and then poses exactly this question. The subsequent gluing discussion in Section 5 sharpens what 'complete intersection' means in the authors' intended context, but it is contextual rather than an explicitly proved equivalent reformulation of the quotient problem itself.
